title: From Phantom to Heist: Andrew Lloyd Webber's Next Musical Is the Wild True Story of the Mona Lisa's Theft
summary: Andrew Lloyd Webber, the composer behind Broadway spectacles like The Phantom of the Opera and Cats, is known for turning fever dreams into musicals. Now he's taking on one of the most surreal true stories in art history: the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa. In a recent interview, Lloyd Webber casually mentioned "the other one" he's working on—a musical about how the world's most famous painting vanished from the Louvre and resurfaced in Italy. The Mona Lisa, a 30-inch-tall portrait by Leonardo da Vinci, was already attracting love letters from admirers in the early 1900s. To protect it, the Louvre encased it in glass. One of the workers on that job was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian glazier and housepainter. He knew exactly how to remove the painting from its frame. On August 21, 1911, when the museum was closed, Peruggia—possibly with accomplices—put on a worker's smock, lifted the Mona Lisa off the wall, and carried it to a stairwell. There, he separated the canvas from its heavy frame and walked out. The theft wasn't discovered for 28 hours, when an artist arrived to sketch the painting and found an empty wall. At first, museum officials assumed it had been taken down for photography. Panic set in only after they found the discarded frame. The investigation was chaotic. Police questioned Pablo Picasso, who was living in Paris at the time. They even interviewed Peruggia at his apartment, where he had stashed the painting in a trunk, but he didn't arouse suspicion. For two years, the Mona Lisa was nowhere to be found. Meanwhile, thousands of curious visitors—including Franz Kafka—flocked to the Louvre just to stare at the blank space where the painting once hung. The theft made the Mona Lisa a global sensation. Before it was stolen, the painting wasn't even the most famous in its gallery. Its absence transformed it into an icon. In late 1913, Peruggia contacted an art dealer in Italy and demanded a ransom. He claimed he wanted to return the painting to its "home country" since da Vinci was Italian. The dealer alerted police, and Peruggia was arrested. Many Italians hailed him as a hero. Lloyd Webber, already juggling a musical based on the film The Illusionist and a queer ballroom reimagining of Cats, says he's going away to write this new show. With his flair for spectacle, the Mona Lisa heist could become the most thrilling musical about a painting ever staged.
why_it_matters: This story shows how a single crime can transform an artwork into a global symbol, raising questions about cultural ownership and how fame is often shaped by loss and mystery. It also reveals that even the most famous icons have unexpected origins, a reminder that history can be rewritten by one daring act.

background_read: Before the theft, the Mona Lisa was just one of many Renaissance portraits at the Louvre—the world-renowned Paris museum that once was a royal palace.
Andrew Lloyd Webber (who created blockbuster musicals like Cats and The Phantom of the Opera in the 1980s) has a knack for turning improbable historical events into theatrical spectacles.

The painting's disappearance in 1911, carried out by an Italian housepainter named Vincenzo Peruggia, exposed how lax museum security was at the time; it took over a day for anyone to notice it was missing.
The resulting media frenzy turned the work into a global celebrity, a pattern repeated with other art heists like the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum theft in 1990.
Peruggia's patriotic claim—that he was returning the painting to Italy—revealed ongoing tensions over cultural heritage and ownership.

perspectives.description: For Andrew Lloyd Webber, the heist is a gift: a larger-than-life true story that naturally lends itself to theatrical spectacle, blending humor, intrigue, and a touch of patriotism. Fans of musical theater can look forward to a show that turns a bizarre art crime into an entertaining cultural event.

Some critics might argue that a musical risks glorifying a thief or trivializing a serious theft. Museums and cultural institutions must still protect artifacts; Peruggia's act, while bizarre, was still a crime that deprived the public of a masterpiece for two years.

The theft reveals how fame is socially constructed: before 1911, the Mona Lisa was not the world's most famous painting; its absence and the media storm created its mystique. This pattern—scarcity and scandal driving public interest—repeats in everything from stolen gems to leaked celebrity photos.

As Lloyd Webber develops the musical, it could spark renewed interest in art security and repatriation debates. The show might encourage young people to think about why some artworks become global icons while others remain obscure, and how stories shape value.
